# Getting Started

Mayon is a learning app you run yourself, on your own computer. This guide takes you from a fresh machine to your first conversation — no programming experience is needed, and every term is explained the first time it appears. (If you want to develop Mayon itself, see [Building from source](../how-to/building.qmd).)

## What you are setting up

Mayon runs entirely on your own computer, and there is no account to create. That is what keeps your chats, notes, and quiz scores private — [data and privacy](../how-to/data-and-privacy.qmd) has the details.

To make this work, Mayon arrives as three small programs — the web app you open in your browser, a helper server, and a database — bundled into *containers*. A **container engine** is a program that downloads and runs containerized apps for you, so a single engine starts all three pieces and you never have to manage them individually. [Docker](https://docs.docker.com/get-docker/) is the most common engine; it is free for personal use.

Chat also needs an **AI provider**: an AI service that generates the replies. You connect one account — either a cloud service with pay-per-use pricing or a free one that runs on your own machine — and Mayon stores its **API key** (a long password that identifies your account) in your browser, on your computer.

## Prerequisites

You'll need three things in place before installing. Each takes only a few minutes.

### 1. A container engine (~2–3 GB download)

- **macOS and Windows:** install [Docker Desktop](https://docs.docker.com/get-docker/). It is free for personal use; larger businesses need a [paid plan](https://www.docker.com/pricing). After installing, open it once and leave it running.
- **Linux:** install [Docker Engine](https://docs.docker.com/get-docker/), or [Podman](https://podman.io/docs/installation), which works just as well.

### 2. An AI provider (required for chat)

Pick one to start; you can add more later and switch at any time.

- **[OpenRouter](https://openrouter.ai/settings/keys)** (easiest) — one account gives you access to hundreds of AI models. You add a small amount of credit and are charged only for what you use; some models are free.
- **[Ollama](https://ollama.com/download)** (free, private) — runs AI models directly on your computer. It costs nothing and works offline, but needs a reasonably capable computer (8 GB of memory or more), and each model download is 1–4 GB.

### 3. A terminal

The **terminal** is a window where you type text commands. You'll use it only once, to run the install command in the next section.

- **macOS:** open the built-in **Terminal** app — [Apple's guide](https://support.apple.com/guide/terminal/welcome/mac) shows how.
- **Windows:** set up [WSL2](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/wsl/install), a Windows feature that gives you an Ubuntu terminal, and use that (see [Windows setup](#windows-setup) below).
- **Linux:** open your distro's terminal.

## Install Mayon

Open your terminal and paste this one line:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://github.com/bendlikeabamboo/mayon/releases/latest/download/install.sh | bash
```

> **What this command does:** it downloads Mayon's install script from GitHub and runs it. The script checks that your container engine is installed, generates a secure random password for the database, writes its settings into a new `~/.mayon` folder in your home directory, and starts Mayon's three containers. Nothing else on your system is changed.

The first run downloads Mayon's programs (several hundred megabytes), so give it a few minutes — and make sure Docker Desktop is running before you start. When it finishes, you'll see `Mayon is up → http://localhost:8080`. The first page load can take another minute while the database prepares itself.

From now on, you manage Mayon with `~/.mayon/install.sh` followed by one of: `stop`, `start`, `restart`, `logs`, `status`, `upgrade`, `uninstall`.

### Windows setup

The installer is a bash script, so on Windows it runs inside [WSL2](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/wsl/install) — an Ubuntu terminal environment provided by Windows — rather than in PowerShell. This setup has been tested end to end: WSL2 with Docker Desktop, the installer run inside Ubuntu, and the app opening in the Windows browser.

1. Open PowerShell as administrator and run `wsl --install`, then restart when prompted. That installs the Ubuntu terminal ([Microsoft's guide](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/wsl/install)). Current Docker Desktop versions need WSL 2.1.5 or newer — check with `wsl --version`, and run `wsl --update` if yours is older.
2. Install [Docker Desktop](https://docs.docker.com/get-docker/) with the [WSL 2 backend](https://docs.docker.com/desktop/wsl/), and in Docker Desktop's settings enable WSL integration for Ubuntu. If you previously installed Docker *inside* the Ubuntu terminal, uninstall that copy first.
3. Open **Ubuntu** from the Start menu and run the install command above inside it.
4. Open **http://localhost:8080** in your usual Windows browser — Docker Desktop forwards the app there automatically.

## First run

Open **http://localhost:8080** in your browser.

The very first screen asks **"Set up security?"** — an offer to protect the app with a password and an authenticator code.

- On your own computer, clicking **Skip** is fine: the app stays open with no sign-in, and you can enable security later under **Settings → Security**.
- If you plan to make Mayon reachable from the internet (for example, on a home server), set up security **before** exposing it.

After that you land on the home dashboard. In the header, a small **DB ready** pill confirms the database came up (a `Runtime: …` line beside it says where the database is running).

If you instead see **"Cannot reach the Mayon server."**, the stack is not running — it may still be starting, or your machine rebooted since. Wait a moment: Mayon keeps checking and recovers on its own. If it does not, run `~/.mayon/install.sh start` in your terminal.

## Connect an AI provider

Open **Settings** (the gear icon in the sidebar) and click **Add provider**. Mayon ships with ready-made settings for many AI services; these two are the recommended starting points.

### Option A: OpenRouter (cloud, pay per use)

1. Create an account at [openrouter.ai](https://openrouter.ai).
2. Add a few dollars of credit at [openrouter.ai/credits](https://openrouter.ai/credits). You are charged only for what you actually use.
3. Create an API key at [openrouter.ai/settings/keys](https://openrouter.ai/settings/keys). While creating it, you can set a **spend cap** — a hard limit on how much that key can ever spend. A modest cap is a safe way to start.
4. In Mayon: **Settings → Add provider → OpenRouter**, pick a model from the list, paste your key, click **Save key**, then click **Set active**.

### Option B: Ollama (free, local, private)

1. Install [Ollama](https://ollama.com/download) on your computer and keep it running.
2. In a terminal, download a small model, for example `ollama pull llama3.2` (about 2 GB — browse the [model library](https://ollama.com/library) for alternatives).
3. In Mayon: **Settings → Add provider → Ollama (local)** and pick the model you pulled. No key is needed.
4. **One required change:** the template prefills the address `http://localhost:11434/api`. Change `localhost` to `host.docker.internal` — that is, use `http://host.docker.internal:11434/api` — because Mayon runs inside a container, where `localhost` does not point at your computer. (Under Podman, use `http://host.containers.internal:11434/api`.) Then click **Set active**.

### What this costs

- **Ollama** is completely free: the model runs on your machine.
- **OpenRouter** and other cloud providers charge per use — typically a few cents for a long conversation — and a per-key spend cap means you can never be charged more than you allowed.
- A personal subscription such as ChatGPT Plus or Claude Pro does not include API access — these services bill API usage separately. That is why this guide links to the API key page rather than your subscription.

## Your first chat

Before your first chat, consider filling in **Settings → Learner profile**: it sets your default knowledge level and preferred teaching style, and Mayon starts each new chat from there.

Back on the home dashboard, click the starter prompt **"Explore a new topic"**: Mayon opens a chat and asks what you are curious about — type anything you want to learn. You can also open the chat list, click **New chat**, and simply start typing. The dashboard keeps your ongoing work one click away: a **Continue learning** card reopens your most recent conversation, and recent chats, labs, and quizzes accumulate below.

When a reply touches something you'd like to dig into, highlight that passage and branch a new conversation from it — see [Chat and branching](chat-and-branching.qmd).
